newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan takes laissez-faire gamble on markets, banks.
newsitem.headline: Japan takes laissez-faire gamble on markets, banks.

text.p: Japan's economic policy makers, once seen as backroom fixers of the financial system, have been preaching laissez faire with the zeal of the converted as they watched bank share prices slide.
The Tokyo stock market's steep slump, some officials say, will finally force financial institutions to do what they should have done before -- restructure and boost profitability.
With the Tokyo market's key 225-share index now hovering just above 18,000 after plunging within a hair's breadth of 17,000 last week, the hands-off stance looks laudable.
The key Nikkei index closed down 54.30 points or 0.30 percent at 18,090.04 on Friday.
But some experts warn that authorities are taking a gamble which risks serious fallout if the share price slide resumes and goes too far, too fast.

"The agenda is to keep this on the front page and force the financial institutions to act," said one foreign financial expert. "But too sudden a slide could unravel things dangerously for some (financial firms)."

Bank shares were among the most battered by the stock market's recent plunge, in part due to a belated realisation that many have lagged both in writing off bad debts inherited from the 1990s collapse of asset prices and in improving profitability with better business strategies.

Worries that Japan's proposed "Big Bang" five-year financial liberalisation plan will further weaken banks also fuelled the falls. So too did the broader market plunge, which erodes banks' unrealised profits on share holdings and would push many into the red should the Nikkei near 15,000.

The government, which in past market crises rode to the rescue, now says publicly that the market should be left to find its own fair value. Privately, some officials are even blunter, arguing banks themselves are to blame for their share price woes and thus must act alone to turn the tide.

But some analysts see a certain irony in the enunciation of a hands-off stance by officials who for years discouraged stronger banks from forcing troubled borrowers to the wall, hedged in their business strategies with regulations and turned a blind eye when some institutions were effectively bankrupt.

Some also wonder whether policy makers, still worried that a sudden spate of failures by financial institutions or their debtors would spark fears of a financial crisis, have really abandoned an interventionist approach.
As recently as last October, Eisuke Sakakibara, the well-known director-general of the finance ministry's international finance bureau, said in a newspaper interview:
"If everything is left up to the market, we lose stability. Those who advocate giving priority to the market, I feel, lack consideration of the point of how merciless the market can be."
But he added, "However, it is true that the wave of marketisation cannot be avoided."
Sharp price declines ahead of the end of the business year on March 31 could pose a serious test for policy-makers.

"If they can keep it between 17,000 and 19,000 until the end of March, that gives some room for manoeuvring," the foreign financial expert said. "But there would be too much damage if it's done too quickly and too brutally."
Some cynics predicted policy mandarins would recant their newfound creed if prospects of painful economic and social fallout from the free-market stance became too great.
"I don't think that the finance ministry has all of a sudden received communion from the high priest of free markets," the foreign economist said.
"It serves their purposes at this time. But if the market were to fall further and threaten the financial sector and the economy, of course they would intervene," he added.
